Risk Factors for Pneumonia Feb. 25, 2026 Español Key points Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs. Pneumonia can cause mild to serious illness in people of all ages. Some people are at increased risk for getting pneumonia. Certain ages, health conditions, and behaviors can increase a person's risk for pneumonia. Talk to a healthcare provider if you have concerns about pneumonia. About risk There are many different germs that can cause pneumonia. The risk for pneumonia can be different for each cause. Keep Reading Causes People at increased risk People are more likely to get pneumonia at certain ages. For adults , those 65 years or older are at increased risk. Risk continues increasing as age increases: an 80-year-old has a higher risk than a 65-year-old adult. For children , those younger than 5 years old are at increased risk. Risk increases for children at younger ages: a 1-year-old has a higher risk than a 4-year-old child. Conditions that can increase risk People who have chronic (ongoing) medical conditions are at increased risk for pneumonia. These can include: Chronic heart disease Chronic liver disease Chronic lung disease

The National Park Service (NPS) was founded in 1916 and just two years later, more visitors came to Yosemite National Park by car than by train. 'Auto touring' national parks quickly became a national past time. Soonafter, a generation of NPS landscape architects and designers set out to design roads as experiences, not just transportation routes. In the process they transformed national parks, the fields of landscape architecture, engineering and design, and the nation. Today, over 5,000 miles of paved roads traverse the national park system, including parkways . A team of dedicated professionals work hard to plan , maintain , and manage a complex road system the nation can be proud of. The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault. His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for." No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules. Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable". pages.description: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
pages.text: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a post-Putin future Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin 20 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Vitaly Shevchenko Chief Analyst, BBC Monitoring Getty Images Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall. More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask. Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war. "I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs." In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word. That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. Always take steps to stay healthy around pet turtles. pages.description: The new Argentine dino might give us clues to what the world was like before the asteroid wiped out their kind.
pages.text: Scientists find a new titanosaur dinosaur species in Patagonia | National Geographic Premium SCIENCE Scientists find a new titanosaur dinosaur species in Patagonia The new Argentine dino might give us clues to what the world was like before the asteroid wiped out their kind. Hundreds of fossils found at a quarry in Northern Patagonia provide a snapshot of what a desert pond ecosystem might have looked like in the late Cretaceous period. Researchers found a previously undiscovered species of titanosaur (illustrated above) among other fossilized creatures at the site. Illustration by Gabriel Lio By Meghie Rodrigues Published March 5, 2025 In Northern Patagonia, paleontologists have unearthed an ancient lagoon ecosystem surrounded by sand dunes and palm trees where prehistoric creatures thrived. Excavations of 78 million year-old rocks, from a quarry just outside General Roca city in Argentina, yielded a treasure trove of 432 fossils belonging to over a hundred animal groups. The majority of the fossils belonged to turtles, but other residents were fish, crocodile relatives, slugs—including the first fossil record of the Neocyclotidae , a family of tropical land snails, and the first record of Leptinaria , a genus of small tropical air-breathing land snails—and dinosaurs . pages.text: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic By Craig Welch Photographs by Thomas Peschak 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. To see all that’s hopeful and appalling about the way we treat sea turtles , there’s no better place to start than the Burj Al Arab Jumeirah hotel. This shimmering tower of blue and white glass is shaped like the jib of a sailboat bound for shore. It rose two decades ago on an artificial island amid the steel forest of construction cranes that is Dubai, part of the United Arab Emirates. A royal suite, at 8,396 square feet, comes with a private cinema and 17 pillow options. A weekend stay can top $50,000. I have come here, though, to see its nonpaying guests. ( Saving Sea Turtles) Passing a fleet of white Rolls-Royces, I meet British expat marine biologist David Robinson. We take an elevator down to a parking garage and walk by Lamborghinis to our destination: a labyrinth of pipes and plastic pools, the intensive care unit of an elaborate marine turtle hospital. In one tub a green sea turtle struggles with internal organ damage. One floor up, sick, critically endangered hawksbills fill aquariums. Blood seeps from a dying leatherback harpooned by an indigenous hunter near Indonesia’s Kei Islands. Leatherbacks are the largest of the seven sea turtle species and one of the most imperiled. The West Pacific population has fewer than a thousand females. A flatback sea turtle kicks up sand while digging a nest on Crab Island, off Australia’s northeast coast. As the search engine used by thousands of federal websites, SearchGov supports more than 200 million searches a year. SearchGov shares its history with USA.gov , beginning when internet entrepreneur Eric Brewer donated a powerful search engine to the government. pages.description: Thousands of years ago, Florida’s coastline extended as much as 100 miles out beyond its present edge. Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America.
pages.text: Searching the Seabed for Florida’s Ice Age Societies | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT Searching the Seabed for Florida’s Ice Age Societies Thousands of years ago, Florida’s coastline extended as much as 100 miles out beyond its present edge. Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America. Archaeologists are diving the coastline that stretches from Texas to Florida to find artifacts from tribes that once lived there thousands of years ago—like these arrowheads from McFadden Beach, just outside present-day Houston. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photo (Composite): Sepia Times/Universal Images Group, Getty Images; Melanie J. Stright, 1999 dissertation, U.S. Department of the Interior Minerals Management Service By Nicolás Rivero Published October 23, 2026 Five miles off Florida’s coast, in a sandy pit on the seafloor near a coral reef, archaeologist Morgan Smith picked up a stone tool someone dropped on dry land 7,000 years ago. It was December 2024, and Smith, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, was diving on an underwater mission to find signs of ancient human life. He sifted through 30 inches of sand and crushed seashells, down to a layer of blue-gray clay silt that could only have formed in a terrestrial environment. pages.text: See how we’re reimagining dinosaurs in today’s ‘golden age’ of paleontology | National Geographic This story appears in the October 2020 issue of National Geographic magazine. On a chilly January afternoon, Susannah Maidment stands on the shore of a London lake, staring down a pack of dinosaurs. Maidment, a curator at the U.K.’s Natural History Museum, has come with me to tour Crystal Palace Park, which in 1854 included the world’s first public dinosaur showcase. The sculptures were a smash hit at their unveiling and sparked the dinomania that’s been with us ever since. More than a century before Steven Spielberg dazzled the world with Jurassic Park , the Crystal Palace dinosaurs drew two million visitors a year for three decades straight, and Charles Dickens name-dropped one in his novel Bleak House . ( Paleontologists Reveal the Identity of ‘Predator X’) To grant us a detailed look at these 166-year-old monuments, Ellinor Michel and Sarah Jayne Slaughter, trustees with the nonprofit Friends of Crystal Palace Dinosaurs, guide us through a metal gate to the banks of the lake, where we don waders to make our crossing. I misjudge my first step and fall into the water, clambering onto the island’s shore, dripping wet and smelling of pond scum. “Welcome to Dinosaur Island!” Slaughter exclaims, grinning from ear to ear. Some 166 million years ago in what is now Oxfordshire County, England, the ground trembled with the footfalls of the first dinosaur to be scientifically described, Megalosaurus. pages.description: The islands of Amantaní and Taquile on the Peruvian side of Lake Titicaca are rich in tradition and renowned for their textile heritage, which can be experienced during a homestay. Visitors might be left breathless by the landscape, too — at an altitude of 3,812 metres, Titicaca is the world’s highest navigable lake.
pages.text: See Island Weavers at Work in Peru's Lake Titicaca | National Geographic Story and photographs by Annapurna Mellor Published September 5, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The island of Amantaní is home to around 4,000 people, divided among 10 communities, including several textile producers. Annapurna Mellor (Top) (Left) and Annapurna Mellor (Bottom) (Right) The Ruta de Circunvalación trail circles the island, with stone arches marking the entrance to each village. Annapurna Mellor Shaped by centuries of terraced farming, the landscape is dotted with native flora, including the vibrant cantuta, Peru’s national flower. Its vibrant red blooms adorn the blouse of Pilar Rosmery Yucra Quispe, a weaver from the island’s Pueblo community. Annapurna Mellor (Top) (Left) and Annapurna Mellor (Bottom) (Right) As well as producing traditional textiles, she runs a homestay, Tikawasi, with her husband, Jose Luis. Annapurna Mellor Textile traditions are safeguarded by Unesco Intangible Cultural Heritage status on the neighbouring island of Taquile. Annapurna Mellor Its inhabitants spin wool and knit in their homes before bringing their goods to the central cooperative in the main square to be sold. Annapurna Mellor The square is the heart of community life, hosting festivals and weddings, as well as daily dance performances for visitors. Instead, they faced a society that was remained divided. Segregation was the rule— ”separate but equal.” Each state was left to decide what that meant. Different practices ensued. Public examples came to light in restaurants, buses, trains, and finally schools. Segregation ended when the US Supreme Court ruled that “separate but equal” had no place in schools. (NPS photo) An Unprecedented Attack On the morning of September 11, 2001, terrorists launched an unprecedented attack on the United States using hijacked commercial airliners. At 8:45 am American Airlines Flight 11 carrying 92 people from Boston to Los Angeles crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York City. Eighteen minutes later, United Airlines Flight 175, with 65 passengers and crew also headed toward California, hit the South Tower. At 9:40 am ET American Airlines Flight 77 carrying 64 people and 30,000 pounds of aviation fuel for its flight from Dulles to Los Angeles crashed into the Pentagon. American Airlines Flight 93 with 40 passengers and crew on their way to San Francisco crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at 10:10 am ET. What scientific and technical information supports reviews? What Are Particulate Matter (PM) Air Quality Standards? National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for PM pollution specify a maximum amount of PM to be present in outdoor air. There are different standards for PM 10 and PM 2.5 (see Particulate Matter (PM) Basics to learn about particle types). Limiting PM pollution in the air protects human health and the environment. See NAAQS for PM for an in-depth explanation of the current PM standards, including Federal Register citations and fact sheets. How Are PM Standards Developed and Reviewed? The Clean Air Act requires EPA to set national air quality standards for particulate matter, as one of the six criteria pollutants considered harmful to public health and the environment. The law also requires EPA to periodically review the standards to ensure that they provide adequate health and environmental protection, and to update those standards as necessary. With Shoshone Falls as a dramatic backdrop, Idaho added its voice to coordinated readings across all 50 states, each of the five Territories, DC, Midway, Wake, Palmyra and all seven continents in honor of the Declaration’s first public readings 250 years ago. Participants pose with the Great American Expedition flag which helps highlight the people, places, and stories that define America’s public lands heritage. Even in mid‑construction, the future overlook proved a powerful and symbolic setting. pages.description: Food producers have welcomed a draft deal between the UK and EU that could remove export checks.
pages.text: Shellfish firms hope EU export deal will 'lift a burden' Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Shellfish firms hope EU deal will 'lift a burden' 7 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Paul Murphy East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire climate and environment correspondent BBC Jo Ackers, from the Independent Shellfishermen's Co-Operative, says exports currently have to be signed off by a vet Food producers have welcomed a draft deal between the UK and the EU which could remove checks on exports that were put in place after Brexit. The agreement should mean savings for the shellfish industry in Bridlington, East Yorkshire, which exports lobster and crab to France, Spain and Portugal and generates at least £10m for the local economy. Jo Ackers, from the Independent Shellfisherman's Co-operative, said it would "lift a burden" from businesses exporting produce. "All of our exports have needed to be signed off by vets because they are live exports and this involves significant expense and paperwork," she said. The BBC understands a 200-page draft text for a so-called SPS (sanitary and phytosanitary) agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels . Since the UK formally left the EU in January 2020, many food exports have needed extra certificates to confirm the product meets the health requirements of the destination country. pages.description: Business owners say they are losing thousands of pounds and help is "well overdue".
pages.text: Shoplifting measures welcomed by Birmingham traders Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Shoplifting measures welcomed by traders 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Bob Hockenhull West Midlands Getty Images The government pilot in the West Midlands will focus on prolific offenders Shopkeepers in the West Midlands have welcomed the announcement of new measures to cut shoplifting. The region is one of 16 police force areas chosen as part of a government pilot to target prolific retail offenders, which could see persistent thieves tagged and banned from high streets. Mani Gill, vice-chair of the Soho Road Business Improvement District (BID), Birmingham, said shoplifting was a daily occurrence, with small businesses least able to absorb the costs. Alex Goss, lead for retail crime at the National Police Chief's Council , said he welcomed the pilot to tackle prolific retail crime offenders "who continue to cause harm to businesses, retail workers and local communities". The new measures announced by the Home Secretary on Wednesday will focus on about 500 of the country's most prolific offenders, who the government said were "responsible for a disproportionate amount of shop theft". It said they could face restrictions on their movements including the use of GPS tags, along with being banned from the high street.
